entries.text: Pioneer: a word for those who go first. And the name was no accident.
March 1972. A small probe, no bigger than a car, set out for the outer planets.
Within eleven hours it crossed the Moon’s orbit. Leaving Earth, it was the fastest machine ever launched.
It spins slowly, like a top. That steady turning keeps the probe stable on its long journey.
Far from the Sun, sunlight is faint. So it carried RTGs: generators turning plutonium’s heat into electricity.
Mars fell behind. Ahead lay a place no one had ever crossed: the asteroid belt.
Nobody knew if anything could pass. Some feared a single collision would end the mission.
Imagine the fear: a path crowded with rocks, packed close together...
In real life, the rocks lie vast distances apart. The route passed millions of kilometres from the nearest.
The detectors found only fine dust.
After seven months, Pioneer emerged on the far side, unharmed. The belt could be crossed.
By November 1973, Jupiter, largest of the planets, was in sight.
A world so vast that eleven Earths could stand side by side across its face.
Pioneer began taking pictures from 25 million kilometres away.
Yet a command and its reply could take up to an hour and a half.
Pioneer had no camera like the one in your phone.
With each turn, it saw just one thin line of Jupiter, in only two colours: red and blue.
Red light built the first picture, one line at a time. Now blue: the same patient turning.
A second picture takes shape, again one thin line at a time.
Red and blue came from the instrument. The third colour would be worked out on Earth.
Pioneer never saw green. Computers on Earth worked it out, and Jupiter appeared in colour.
Some pictures were lost, Io’s among them. But so much reached us.
This is Ganymede, seen by Pioneer 10 in 1973: close-ups of the Solar System’s largest moon.
These pictures were sharper than anything a telescope on Earth could offer.
Closer it came, passing Jupiter’s great moons and photographing Ganymede up close.
Jupiter is wrapped in radiation thousands of times stronger than Earth’s.
It absorbed over a thousand times a fatal human dose. Unwanted commands arose; backups were ready.
4 December 1973: Pioneer 10 became the first to fly past Jupiter.
About 130,000 km above the clouds: three times closer than the Moon to us.
Jupiter’s gravity bent its path and gave it the boost to travel beyond the planets.
It found Jupiter’s radiation fiercer than expected, which shaped Voyager’s design.
No return journey: Pioneer was bound for the stars, carrying a letter on a gold-coloured plaque.
First, hydrogen, the commonest atom in the Universe: our ruler.
Then pulsars, blinking stars that show where the Sun lies.
The Solar System: Pioneer leaving the third planet, Earth.
Beside it, Pioneer’s own outline, to show our size.
And before it, two figures. One of them is waving hello.
A gold-coloured aluminium plaque: a letter for an encounter that may never happen.
Built to last twenty-one months, Pioneer carried on: it crossed the distance of Saturn’s orbit in 1976 and Uranus’s in 1979.
13 June 1983: it crossed the distance of Neptune’s orbit, its instruments still working normally.
Year by year the generators weakened. The instruments took turns, and one by one were switched off.
In 1998, Voyager 1 overtook it to become the most distant human-made object, travelling in another direction.
Pioneer had shown the way. Now Earth had to listen from ever farther away.
Its signal was now fainter than a whisper. Could Earth’s antennas still hear it?
March 2002. Thirty years after launch, Pioneer was still answering.
April 2002. The last data from its instruments reached Earth.
January 2003. A last faint signal, from twelve billion kilometres away, took over eleven hours to reach us.
February 2003. Earth listened once more, and no signal was detected.
Without enough power to reach us, Pioneer 10 fell silent. But it did not stop.
It travels on, towards the red star Aldebaran: a journey measured in millions of years.
Built to last twenty-one months, it lasted more than thirty years.
And the name was no accident: first to the outer planets, first across the asteroid belt, first to fly past Jupiter.
Pioneer: one who goes first. Every great journey begins with someone who goes first. Pioneer 10 went first, for us all.
The first visit to Jupiter. Turn signals into images and listen to a thirty-year journey.
